tasks.prompt: Order the post incident review and recovery sequence after a major emergency.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 4 water treatment system used for study. All sequences follow standard practice in the cited sources for Ontario drinking water operations under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard.
tasks.configuration: Scope: from emergency stand down to a stronger system than before the event.

cards.label: Confirm the emergency is over and essential services and water quality are stable
Restore normal staffing, replenish consumed resources, and repair temporary measures
Collect logs, records, and accounts from all responding teams while memories are fresh
Analyse what worked, what failed, and the root causes of any harm or delay
Agree improvement actions with owners and dates and update the emergency plan
Share the review with senior management, the owner, and responding partners as appropriate

tasks.explanation: Recovery restores service first, then learning improves the system. Updating the plan while evidence is fresh is what makes the next response better.

tasks.prompt: Order the ministry inspection readiness sequence for a drinking water system.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 4 water treatment system used for study. All sequences follow standard practice in the cited sources for Ontario drinking water operations under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard.
tasks.configuration: Scope: preparing for a scheduled provincial inspection under Ontario Regulation 170/03.

cards.label: Confirm the inspection scope, dates, and the records period the inspector will review
Audit sampling, monitoring, and reporting records for completeness and accuracy
Walk the plant and distribution system to find and correct housekeeping and labelling gaps
Verify operator certification records, logbooks, and contingency plans are current and retrievable
Brief staff on inspection conduct, honest answers, and who escorts the inspector
Host the inspection, track every request and finding, and begin corrections immediately where possible

tasks.explanation: Readiness is a records and field audit done before the inspector arrives. Tracking requests during the visit prevents findings being lost.

tasks.prompt: Order the annual compliance reporting leadership sequence.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 4 water treatment system used for study. All sequences follow standard practice in the cited sources for Ontario drinking water operations under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard.
tasks.configuration: Scope: preparing the annual report and summary report required for the system.

cards.label: Compile the year production, sampling, adverse incident, and corrective action records
Verify the data against laboratory reports, logbooks, and continuous monitoring records
Draft the reports in the required format with explanations for any incidents or exceedances
Review the drafts with the overall responsible operator and senior management for accuracy
Submit the reports by the regulatory deadlines and provide them to the owner and the public as required
File the submitted reports and record lessons for improving data collection next year

tasks.explanation: Verification against source records precedes drafting claims. Submission by deadline and public availability are both compliance requirements, not courtesies.

tasks.prompt: Order the adverse water quality incident leadership sequence.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 4 water treatment system used for study. All sequences follow standard practice in the cited sources for Ontario drinking water operations under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard.
tasks.configuration: Scope: senior handling of an adverse test result from notification to final closure.

cards.label: Receive the adverse result and confirm the sample details and result validity with the laboratory
Make the immediate verbal notifications to the health unit and the ministry as regulation requires
Issue any required public notices and direct resampling and corrective actions
Submit the written adverse report within the required timeline with actions taken
Collect resample results and confirm the issue is resolved with the health unit
File the complete incident record and review the event for preventive actions

tasks.explanation: Immediate verbal notification cannot wait for perfect information. Written reports and resampling then prove the corrective action worked.

tasks.prompt: Order the regulatory sampling program leadership sequence for a new operating year.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 4 water treatment system used for study. All sequences follow standard practice in the cited sources for Ontario drinking water operations under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard.
tasks.configuration: Scope: setting up the full Regulation 170/03 sampling program for the year ahead.

cards.label: Review the regulation, licence, and permit sampling requirements for every parameter and location
Build the annual sampling calendar with frequencies, locations, and responsible staff
Confirm laboratory arrangements, bottles, preservatives, and courier schedules for each sample type
Brief samplers on locations, techniques, chain of custody, and adverse result duties
Track completion monthly and reschedule any missed sample within its required window
Review program results quarterly and adjust locations or frequencies where evidence supports it

tasks.explanation: Requirements define the calendar, and monthly tracking catches misses while they can still be corrected. Quarterly review turns sampling into information, not only compliance.

tasks.prompt: Order the corrective action sequence after a ministry inspection order is issued.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 4 water treatment system used for study. All sequences follow standard practice in the cited sources for Ontario drinking water operations under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard.
tasks.configuration: Scope: responding to a provincial officers order with binding deadlines.

cards.label: Read the order carefully and confirm every requirement, deadline, and reporting duty
Brief senior management and the owner on the order, its risks, and the resources needed
Prepare a compliance plan assigning each requirement an owner, actions, and interim milestones
Implement the plan with priority on any requirement affecting drinking water safety
Provide progress reports to the inspector as the order requires and keep evidence of each step
Confirm in writing when every requirement is met and request closure of the order

tasks.explanation: The order, not preference, sets the priorities and deadlines. Written confirmation and evidence are needed because the utility must prove compliance, not assume it.

tasks.prompt: Order the drinking water works permit and licence amendment sequence.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 4 water treatment system used for study. All sequences follow standard practice in the cited sources for Ontario drinking water operations under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard.
tasks.configuration: Scope: amending approvals for a significant change to the drinking water system.

cards.label: Confirm the proposed change needs an amendment and identify the approval instruments affected
Prepare the technical description, drawings, and supporting studies for the change
Review the application internally for consistency with the operational plan and source protection requirements
Submit the application and respond to ministry questions and information requests
Receive the amended approvals and update procedures, drawings, and staff training to match
Implement the change only within the conditions of the amended approvals

tasks.explanation: Work must stay within existing approvals until the amendment is granted. Updating procedures and training makes the new approval real in daily operations.

tasks.prompt: Order the source protection plan implementation sequence for a water system.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 4 water treatment system used for study. All sequences follow standard practice in the cited sources for Ontario drinking water operations under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard.
tasks.configuration: Scope: carrying out the system duties under the local source protection plan.

cards.label: Identify the vulnerable areas, threats, and policies that apply to the system sources
Assign each applicable policy an owner and the actions the utility must complete
Complete risk management, signage, monitoring, and reporting duties by their required dates
Train operators on spill response and land use concerns inside the vulnerable areas
Report implementation progress to the source protection authority as required
Review the duties whenever the source protection plan or the system sources change

tasks.explanation: Duties flow from the plan policies, so identifying them accurately comes first. Reporting and review keep protection active as land use and plans change.

tasks.prompt: Order the lead and corrosion control program leadership sequence.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 4 water treatment system used for study. All sequences follow standard practice in the cited sources for Ontario drinking water operations under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard.
tasks.configuration: Scope: managing the regulatory lead sampling and corrosion control duties for the system.

cards.label: Confirm the sampling requirements, locations, and schedule that apply to the system this period
Collect samples exactly to protocol, including plumbing and distribution samples as required
Review results against the standard and identify any locations or patterns of concern
Notify the required parties and the public of results and any required corrective steps
Implement or adjust corrosion control treatment where results show it is needed
Track results over successive periods and report the program status to senior management

tasks.explanation: Protocol exact sampling comes before any conclusion about lead levels. Treatment adjustment follows evidence, and trending shows whether control is working.

tasks.prompt: Order the records management sequence for regulatory compliance evidence.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 4 water treatment system used for study. All sequences follow standard practice in the cited sources for Ontario drinking water operations under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard.
tasks.configuration: Scope: ensuring compliance records are complete, retrievable, and retained as required.

cards.label: Inventory the record types the regulation, licence, and DWQMS require the system to keep
Set retention periods, storage locations, and access rules for each record type
Check current records for gaps, unsigned entries, and misfiling and correct what can be corrected
Train staff on contemporaneous recording, corrections, and logbook standards
Audit retrievability by requesting sample records and timing their production
Review the records system annually and after any inspection finding about records

tasks.explanation: You cannot manage records you have not inventoried. The retrievability audit tests the system the way an inspector will.

tasks.prompt: Order the compliance data verification sequence before a regulatory submission.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 4 water treatment system used for study. All sequences follow standard practice in the cited sources for Ontario drinking water operations under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard.
tasks.configuration: Scope: senior verification of monitoring data before it is submitted to the ministry.

cards.label: Extract the submission data set and confirm the period, parameters, and locations are complete
Reconcile the data against laboratory reports and continuous monitoring records
Investigate and resolve discrepancies, documenting any corrections and their reasons
Confirm adverse incidents in the period are all reported and cross referenced
Obtain the overall responsible operator review and sign off of the verified data
Submit the data, file the submission copy, and record the submission confirmation

tasks.explanation: Reconciliation against source records catches errors while they can still be fixed. Sign off after verification gives the submission accountable ownership.

tasks.prompt: Order the asset management plan development sequence for a water utility.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 4 water treatment system used for study. All sequences follow standard practice in the cited sources for Ontario drinking water operations under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard.
tasks.configuration: Scope: building a plan that links asset condition, service levels, risk, and funding.

cards.label: Define the scope of assets covered and the levels of service the utility commits to deliver
Build the asset inventory with age, condition, capacity, and replacement value information
Assess risks and identify the assets whose failure would most affect service and compliance
Develop lifecycle and renewal strategies with forecast costs for each asset group
Align the plan with the capital forecast, operating budget, and long term financial plan
Obtain owner approval, publish the plan summary, and schedule annual updates

tasks.explanation: Service levels come before spending strategies, because assets exist to deliver service. Owner approval connects the technical plan to funding decisions.

tasks.prompt: Order the asset condition assessment program sequence.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 4 water treatment system used for study. All sequences follow standard practice in the cited sources for Ontario drinking water operations under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard.
tasks.configuration: Scope: rolling program that grades condition across treatment and distribution assets.

cards.label: Select the asset groups due for assessment and the grading scale to be used consistently
Gather maintenance history, failure records, and performance data for each group
Inspect the assets in the field and grade condition with supporting photographs
Enter grades into the asset register and flag assets in poor or critical condition
Report the condition profile and the highest risk assets to senior management
Feed poor condition assets into renewal planning with recommended timing

tasks.explanation: A consistent scale makes grades comparable across years and asset groups. The program succeeds when poor grades change renewal priorities.

tasks.prompt: Order the asset criticality ranking sequence for maintenance and renewal priorities.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 4 water treatment system used for study. All sequences follow standard practice in the cited sources for Ontario drinking water operations under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard.
tasks.configuration: Scope: ranking assets by consequence and likelihood of failure.

cards.label: List the assets and systems to be ranked with their functions in the treatment process
Score consequence of failure for water quality, supply, safety, environment, and cost
Score likelihood of failure using age, condition, and failure history evidence
Combine the scores into a criticality ranking and review outliers with operations staff
Apply the ranking to maintenance frequency, spare parts holdings, and renewal order
Refresh the ranking annually and after any major failure or system change

tasks.explanation: Consequence and likelihood are scored separately before they are combined. Applying the ranking to spares and maintenance is where it changes daily decisions.

tasks.prompt: Order the lifecycle renewal planning sequence for a major asset group.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 4 water treatment system used for study. All sequences follow standard practice in the cited sources for Ontario drinking water operations under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard.
tasks.configuration: Scope: planning renewal of one asset group, for example high lift pumps, over its full life.

cards.label: Establish the current age, condition, performance, and maintenance cost of the group
Estimate remaining useful life and the failure risks in the final years of service
Compare refurbishment, like for like replacement, and upgraded replacement options
Select the preferred strategy and time the renewal before reliability becomes unacceptable
Include the renewal in the capital forecast with procurement lead time allowed
Monitor performance after renewal and record actual life and costs for future planning

tasks.explanation: Remaining life evidence sets the timing window. Recording actual outcomes improves the next lifecycle estimate instead of repeating assumptions.

tasks.prompt: Order the level of service framework development sequence.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 4 water treatment system used for study. All sequences follow standard practice in the cited sources for Ontario drinking water operations under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard.
tasks.configuration: Scope: defining measurable service commitments for council and customers.

cards.label: Identify the service areas customers and regulators care about, such as quality, pressure, and reliability
Set measurable indicators and target levels for each service area with senior management
Confirm current performance against the targets using operating and complaint data
Identify the asset and funding implications of closing any gaps to target
Report performance against the framework to the owner at least annually
Review and adjust targets when expectations, regulations, or funding change materially

tasks.explanation: Targets must be measurable and based on current performance evidence. Annual reporting keeps service promises connected to asset funding.

tasks.prompt: Order the maintenance strategy review sequence from preventive to predictive practice.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 4 water treatment system used for study. All sequences follow standard practice in the cited sources for Ontario drinking water operations under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard.
tasks.configuration: Scope: modernizing maintenance for critical treatment equipment.

cards.label: Analyse work order and failure history to find the equipment causing the most downtime
Classify equipment by criticality and current maintenance approach
Identify where condition monitoring or predictive checks can replace fixed interval tasks
Pilot the revised strategy on one critical equipment group and track failures and costs
Train technicians on the new tasks and update the maintenance system schedules
Adopt the strategy where the pilot proves it and review results annually

tasks.explanation: Failure history shows where the current strategy is failing. A pilot proves predictive tasks work before they replace proven preventive work.

tasks.prompt: Order the critical spare parts program sequence.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 4 water treatment system used for study. All sequences follow standard practice in the cited sources for Ontario drinking water operations under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard.
tasks.configuration: Scope: ensuring spares exist for failures that would stop treatment or supply.

cards.label: List critical equipment and the failure modes that would remove it from service
Identify the parts needed for each failure mode and their supplier lead times
Set stock levels that balance outage risk against inventory cost for each part
Stock, label, and record the parts in the inventory system with reorder points
Review usage and lead times annually and adjust levels for obsolescence
Audit physical stock against records and correct discrepancies found

tasks.explanation: Lead time drives stock decisions, because a cheap part with a long lead time can still cause a long outage. Annual review handles obsolescence before it surprises.

tasks.prompt: Order the asset decommissioning leadership sequence for retired treatment equipment.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 4 water treatment system used for study. All sequences follow standard practice in the cited sources for Ontario drinking water operations under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard.
tasks.configuration: Scope: safely retiring a replaced process unit and removing it from service records.

cards.label: Confirm the replacement is in service and the old asset is no longer needed for any duty
Isolate, drain, clean, and de energize the asset and remove chemicals and residuals
Assess the asset and site for hazardous materials and environmental requirements
Remove or secure the asset and restore the area to a safe condition
Remove the asset from the register, maintenance plans, drawings, and procedures
Record disposal, costs, and any salvage value and close the decommissioning file

tasks.explanation: De energizing and cleaning precede removal work for safety. Removing the asset from drawings and plans prevents future staff trusting records for equipment that no longer exists.

tasks.prompt: Order the capital versus maintenance decision sequence for a failing asset.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 4 water treatment system used for study. All sequences follow standard practice in the cited sources for Ontario drinking water operations under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard.
tasks.configuration: Scope: deciding whether to keep repairing an asset or renew it.

cards.label: Compile the repair history, maintenance cost trend, and downtime caused by the asset
Assess remaining life and the risk that failures will affect compliance or supply
Cost continued maintenance over the next five years including expected major repairs
Cost renewal including capital, installation, and the operating savings it would bring
Compare the options on cost, risk, and service impact and recommend a course of action
Record the decision and, if renewal is chosen, enter the project into the capital forecast

tasks.explanation: Cost comparison without risk comparison favours endless repair. The recorded decision prevents the same debate recurring at every breakdown.

tasks.prompt: Order the asset performance reporting sequence to the owner.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 4 water treatment system used for study. All sequences follow standard practice in the cited sources for Ontario drinking water operations under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard.
tasks.configuration: Scope: annual report connecting asset condition and investment to service outcomes.

cards.label: Compile condition, renewal spending, failure, and service performance data for the year
Compare renewal investment with the level the asset management plan says is required
Highlight assets and risks that grew because renewal was deferred
Present options for the coming year with the service consequences of each funding level
Record owner decisions and direction in the meeting minutes
Update the asset plan and capital forecast to reflect the decisions taken

tasks.explanation: Owners decide funding, so the report must show consequences, not only spending. Recording decisions links the report to next year plan.

tasks.prompt: Order the energy management program launch sequence for a water utility.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 4 water treatment system used for study. All sequences follow standard practice in the cited sources for Ontario drinking water operations under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard.
tasks.configuration: Scope: establishing a managed program to reduce energy use per cubic metre treated.

cards.label: Compile energy use and cost by plant, process area, and pumping station for a baseline year
Set an energy intensity target and assign an energy lead with senior management support
Identify the largest loads and the operational practices that drive them
Approve an action list covering operations, maintenance, and capital measures
Implement the actions in priority order and track energy monthly against the baseline
Report results, savings, and next actions to senior management each quarter

tasks.explanation: A baseline year and a named lead turn good intentions into a program. Monthly tracking against baseline is how savings are proven.

tasks.prompt: Order the energy audit sequence for a treatment plant.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 4 water treatment system used for study. All sequences follow standard practice in the cited sources for Ontario drinking water operations under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard.
tasks.configuration: Scope: detailed audit from data collection to an investment grade opportunity list.

cards.label: Collect utility bills, interval data, equipment inventories, and operating schedules
Walk the plant to observe operating practices, idle equipment, and control settings
Analyse the data to build a load profile and identify peak demand drivers
Quantify each saving opportunity with energy, cost, and implementation effort
Rank opportunities by payback and operational risk and present them to management
Enter approved opportunities into the energy program and track their delivery

tasks.explanation: Observation in the field catches waste that bills alone cannot explain. Ranking by payback and risk lets management fund the right measures first.

tasks.prompt: Order the chemical program strategy review sequence.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 4 water treatment system used for study. All sequences follow standard practice in the cited sources for Ontario drinking water operations under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard.
tasks.configuration: Scope: annual senior review of all treatment chemicals, suppliers, and dosing systems.

cards.label: Compile chemical usage, unit costs, dose performance, and supplier reliability for the year
Review treated water quality outcomes achieved at current doses and products
Test alternate products or suppliers through jar testing and controlled plant trials
Assess storage capacity, delivery reliability, and single source risks for each chemical
Select products and suppliers for the next period through the procurement process
Update dose guidance, contracts, and contingency arrangements for supply interruptions

tasks.explanation: Quality outcomes come before price in the review order. Supply resilience is assessed before contracts are signed, not after a missed delivery.

tasks.prompt: Order the chemical delivery resilience planning sequence.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 4 water treatment system used for study. All sequences follow standard practice in the cited sources for Ontario drinking water operations under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard.
tasks.configuration: Scope: protecting treatment against delayed or failed chemical deliveries.

cards.label: Calculate days of storage on hand for each chemical at maximum and average dose rates
Identify chemicals with short cover, single suppliers, or difficult delivery access
Set minimum stock triggers and reorder points that account for delivery lead times
Arrange alternate suppliers, emergency contacts, and mutual aid options for critical chemicals
Brief operators on conservation dosing and escalation steps if a delivery is missed
Test the arrangements with a tabletop review and update the contingency plan

tasks.explanation: Days of cover at maximum dose is the honest measure of resilience. Triggers and alternates must exist before a delivery fails.

tasks.prompt: Order the chemical dose optimization program sequence across a full plant.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 4 water treatment system used for study. All sequences follow standard practice in the cited sources for Ontario drinking water operations under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard.
tasks.configuration: Scope: coordinated optimization of coagulant, disinfectant, and conditioning chemicals.

cards.label: Establish baseline doses, costs, and treated water quality for each chemical over a representative period
Confirm the water quality targets and limits that optimization must not compromise
Run jar tests and stepwise plant trials to find the lowest effective dose for each chemical
Watch downstream effects, because one chemical change can shift another chemical demand
Adopt the optimized doses into guidance tables linked to raw water conditions
Track dose, cost, and quality monthly and investigate any drift from the optimized values

tasks.explanation: Baselines and quality limits frame the program. Downstream effects are checked because chemicals interact across the process train.

tasks.prompt: Order the pumping energy optimization sequence for high lift and distribution pumping.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 4 water treatment system used for study. All sequences follow standard practice in the cited sources for Ontario drinking water operations under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard.
tasks.configuration: Scope: reducing pumping energy while maintaining storage levels and pressures.

cards.label: Profile pumping energy, flows, pressures, and electricity price periods for the system
Identify pumps operating far from their best efficiency point or against throttled valves
Develop a revised pumping schedule that favours efficient pumps and lower price periods
Trial the schedule while monitoring storage levels, pressures, and water age
Confirm energy savings and that no service or quality indicator has degraded
Adopt the schedule, update pump control settings, and review it seasonally

tasks.explanation: Efficiency and price periods together determine the cheapest compliant schedule. Water age and pressure are monitored because energy savings cannot trade away quality.

tasks.prompt: Order the energy performance contract oversight sequence.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 4 water treatment system used for study. All sequences follow standard practice in the cited sources for Ontario drinking water operations under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard.
tasks.configuration: Scope: senior oversight of a guaranteed savings project delivered by an energy services provider.

cards.label: Agree the baseline, measurement method, and guaranteed savings in the contract before work begins
Review the providers designs and confirm they do not compromise treatment or compliance
Monitor construction and commissioning of the energy measures with plant staff involved
Verify measured savings against the agreed method for the first performance period
Require corrective action from the provider if savings fall short of the guarantee
Report verified savings and contract status to senior management annually

tasks.explanation: The measurement method agreed in advance decides whether savings claims can be trusted. Verification each period enforces the guarantee.

tasks.prompt: Order the chemical storage upgrade program sequence.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 4 water treatment system used for study. All sequences follow standard practice in the cited sources for Ontario drinking water operations under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard.
tasks.configuration: Scope: upgrading bulk chemical storage for safety and regulatory compliance.

cards.label: Assess current storage against containment, ventilation, separation, and eyewash requirements
Rank deficiencies by risk to people, the environment, and treatment continuity
Design upgrades with operations input on delivery access and operator tasks
Plan construction so chemical supply is maintained throughout the work
Commission the upgraded storage with leak testing and updated safety procedures
Train all operators on the new storage, update drawings, and close the project file

tasks.explanation: Risk ranking sets the upgrade order. Supply continuity planning prevents the upgrade itself from interrupting treatment.

tasks.prompt: Order the peak energy demand management sequence.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 4 water treatment system used for study. All sequences follow standard practice in the cited sources for Ontario drinking water operations under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard.
tasks.configuration: Scope: reducing demand charges by controlling when large loads run.

cards.label: Analyse interval data to find when system peaks occur and which loads create them
Identify loads that can be shifted, staggered, or briefly paused without process risk
Set demand targets and alarms that warn operators before a new peak is established
Trial the demand control practices during a typical high demand period
Measure the peak reduction and confirm treatment and storage were not compromised
Formalize the practices in operating procedures and review peak performance monthly

tasks.explanation: Peaks must be understood from interval data before they can be managed. Alarms give operators the warning they need to act in time.

tasks.prompt: Order the chemical inventory and cost control sequence.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 4 water treatment system used for study. All sequences follow standard practice in the cited sources for Ontario drinking water operations under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard.
tasks.configuration: Scope: monthly control cycle linking stock, usage, dose, and cost.

cards.label: Count physical stock and reconcile it with delivery and usage records
Calculate usage per cubic metre treated and cost per cubic metre for each chemical
Compare unit usage with dose guidance for the raw water conditions experienced
Investigate variances caused by dose drift, leaks, spills, or recording errors
Adjust orders and dose guidance and brief operators on any corrections
Report chemical cost and usage trends to senior management with the monthly results

tasks.explanation: Reconciled stock makes usage figures trustworthy. Variance investigation separates real dose problems from simple recording errors.

tasks.prompt: Order the laboratory quality management system review sequence.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 4 water treatment system used for study. All sequences follow standard practice in the cited sources for Ontario drinking water operations under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard.
tasks.configuration: Scope: annual senior review of the laboratory quality manual and its performance.

cards.label: Compile quality indicators including control failures, audit findings, and turnaround times
Review the quality manual against current methods, instruments, and regulatory requirements
Assess staff training and competency records for every test the laboratory performs
Identify recurring quality problems and their root causes from the indicator data
Approve updates to the manual, methods, and training plans with assigned owners
Verify the updates are in use at the next internal quality audit

tasks.explanation: Indicators and competency records show whether the system works in practice. Verification at audit prevents manual updates that never reach the bench.

tasks.prompt: Order the laboratory audit readiness sequence for an external quality assessment.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 4 water treatment system used for study. All sequences follow standard practice in the cited sources for Ontario drinking water operations under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard.
tasks.configuration: Scope: preparing the laboratory for an external accreditation or client audit visit.

cards.label: Confirm the assessment scope, standards, and schedule with the assessing body
Run an internal audit of methods, records, calibrations, and quality controls
Correct documentation and record gaps found and brief analysts on audit conduct
Verify every instrument calibration and standard is current and traceable
Host the assessment, provide requested records, and record all findings raised
Complete corrective actions and submit evidence within the assessors required timelines

tasks.explanation: Traceability and current calibrations are checked before the visit because they cannot be created on the day. Findings enter the same corrective discipline as internal ones.

tasks.prompt: Order the quality control chart program sequence for a key laboratory test.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 4 water treatment system used for study. All sequences follow standard practice in the cited sources for Ontario drinking water operations under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard.
tasks.configuration: Scope: establishing statistical control monitoring for a compliance test method.

cards.label: Select the control material and the test frequency for routine quality control samples
Collect enough control results to establish a reliable mean and control limits
Plot results on the control chart for every analytical run and apply the acceptance rules
Stop and investigate reporting when a result breaks a control rule
Identify the cause, correct it, and reanalyse affected samples before results are released
Review charts monthly for trends that warn of drift before limits are broken

tasks.explanation: Control limits need enough data to be meaningful. Monthly trend review catches slow drift that single run rules can miss.

tasks.prompt: Order the proficiency testing program sequence for laboratory analysts.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 4 water treatment system used for study. All sequences follow standard practice in the cited sources for Ontario drinking water operations under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard.
tasks.configuration: Scope: annual cycle of external proficiency samples from receipt to evaluated results.

cards.label: Enrol in proficiency rounds for every accredited or compliance parameter the laboratory reports
Receive the samples and analyse them exactly like routine samples, without special treatment
Submit results by the deadline and record the analysts and methods used
Compare the laboratory scores with the assigned values when reports are issued
Investigate any unsatisfactory score for analyst, method, or instrument causes
Complete corrective actions and verify improvement in the next proficiency round

tasks.explanation: Proficiency samples only test real performance when they are treated as routine. Unsatisfactory scores require cause investigation, not only disappointment.

tasks.prompt: Order the method validation sequence before a new laboratory method is used for reporting.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 4 water treatment system used for study. All sequences follow standard practice in the cited sources for Ontario drinking water operations under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard.
tasks.configuration: Scope: proving a new or changed method is fit for compliance reporting.

cards.label: Confirm the method scope, reporting limits, and quality criteria the validation must meet
Prepare validation samples covering the working range, including blanks and spikes
Run the validation batches and calculate precision, bias, and detection performance
Compare the results with the acceptance criteria and the requirements of the standard method
Approve the method for use, update the quality manual, and train and assess analysts
Place the method under routine quality control and review its early performance

tasks.explanation: Validation evidence comes before approval for reporting. Early routine performance is reviewed because validation conditions differ from daily workload.

tasks.prompt: Order the chain of custody and data integrity sequence for compliance samples.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 4 water treatment system used for study. All sequences follow standard practice in the cited sources for Ontario drinking water operations under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard.
tasks.configuration: Scope: protecting sample and result integrity from collection to reported result.

cards.label: Label samples uniquely at collection and complete the chain of custody form at handover
Transport and store samples within temperature and holding time requirements and log their receipt
Analyse samples under the assigned identifiers and record raw data contemporaneously
Review calculations, transcriptions, and quality controls before results are authorized
Report results through the controlled system with an audit trail for any corrections
Archive raw data, custody forms, and reports so the full history can be reconstructed

tasks.explanation: Integrity is built at each handover, not reconstructed later. The archive test is whether an auditor can rebuild the result from raw data alone.

tasks.prompt: Order the laboratory corrective action sequence after a quality control failure.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 4 water treatment system used for study. All sequences follow standard practice in the cited sources for Ontario drinking water operations under Ontario Regulation 170/03 and the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard.

tasks.prompt: At utility scale, ultrafiltration Rack C normalized permeability fell 22 percent in 3 weeks while Racks A, B, and D held steady at the same flux.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 4 water treatment utility record. Steady operation unless noted. Archived plant, laboratory, and management records are available for review.

evidence.label: All four racks run at 45 L per m2 per h and share the same feed header.
Feed temperature is stable and temperature corrected permeability still fell on Rack C only.
Rack C feed ATP rose from 180 to 2100 relative light units after a reservoir algae increase, while other racks stayed below 250.
Chemically enhanced backwash recovery on Rack C fell from 90 percent to 58 percent, while other racks stayed near 89 percent.
A bench chlorine soak of a Rack C fibre restored 85 percent of lost permeability, while an acid soak restored only 10 percent.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Irreversible mineral scaling is affecting all four racks equally
A common feed pump failure is starving all racks of flow
The Rack C pressure transmitter has drifted and no real fouling exists
Biofouling concentrated on Rack C is driving its permeability loss

inference.explanation: The loss is rack specific at shared flux and temperature, which rules out a common pump or plant wide scaling cause. High ATP, poor backwash recovery, and strong chlorine soak recovery with weak acid recovery fit biofouling. A drifted transmitter would not change backwash recovery or bench soak results.

nextClue.prompt: Which record best confirms biofouling on Rack C?

options.label: Archived common feed pump amperage log
Archived raw water hardness log
Archived rack by rack ATP trend paired with temperature corrected permeability trend

nextClue.explanation: The correct record directly tests the supported explanation against the alternatives.

clueText.nc-a: Pump amperage was steady across racks and does not separate Rack C.
clueText.nc-b: Hardness was steady and does not explain a rack specific biological signal.
clueText.nc-c: ATP on Rack C rose as its corrected permeability fell, while the other racks stayed flat on both measures.

tasks.prompt: A six train reverse osmosis fleet lost 14 percent of total capacity, and normalized data show the loss sits entirely in Trains 5 and 6 tail stages.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 4 water treatment utility record. Steady operation unless noted. Archived plant, laboratory, and management records are available for review.

evidence.label: Trains 1 to 4 normalized permeate flow is unchanged, while Trains 5 and 6 Stage 2 flow fell 20 percent.
Trains 5 and 6 were switched to a higher recovery of 84 percent last month, while Trains 1 to 4 stayed at 76 percent.
Concentrate silica and calcium indices exceed saturation at 84 percent recovery but sit below saturation at 76 percent.
Antiscalant dose was not increased when recovery was raised on Trains 5 and 6.
Returning Trains 5 and 6 to 76 percent in a 2 week trial stopped further flow loss with no other changes.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: All six trains have reached membrane end of life at once
Feed salinity rose for the whole plant
The higher recovery on Trains 5 and 6 pushed tail stage concentrate past saturation, causing scaling
Biofouling in the lead stages is blocking the whole fleet

inference.explanation: Only the trains moved to higher recovery lost flow, and only in tail stages where concentrate is strongest. Saturation indices cross limits only at the higher recovery, and the return trial stopped the loss. Lead stage biofouling and fleet wide end of life do not fit a two train tail pattern.

nextClue.prompt: Which record best confirms the recovery related scaling?

options.label: Archived feed conductivity log for the whole plant
Archived recovery setting log paired with normalized Stage 2 flow by train
Archived lead stage differential pressure log

nextClue.explanation: The correct record directly tests the supported explanation against the alternatives.

clueText.nc-a: Plant feed conductivity was steady and does not explain a two train pattern.
clueText.nc-b: Stage 2 loss began when recovery rose on Trains 5 and 6 and stopped when recovery returned to 76 percent.
clueText.nc-c: Lead stage pressures stayed normal throughout the period.

tasks.prompt: Fleet wide review shows membrane replacement is proposed for all 40 modules, but age and performance records differ sharply by bank.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 4 water treatment utility record. Steady operation unless noted. Archived plant, laboratory, and management records are available for review.

evidence.label: Banks 1 and 2, age 11 years, show corrected permeability at 62 percent of baseline and failed integrity tests on 6 modules.
Banks 3 and 4, age 6 years, show corrected permeability at 94 percent of baseline and pass all integrity tests.
Cleaning restores less than 15 percent of lost permeability on Banks 1 and 2, but over 80 percent on Banks 3 and 4.
Permeate quality from Banks 3 and 4 meets all targets, while Banks 1 and 2 need blending to hold turbidity targets.
A pilot replacement of 4 modules in Bank 1 restored that section to 96 percent of baseline permeability.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: No modules need replacement because cleaning was attempted
Only Banks 1 and 2 have reached end of useful life, so staged replacement of those banks is supported, not a fleet wide change out
All 40 modules must be replaced because one purchase is simpler
Banks 3 and 4 are the failed banks and should be replaced first

inference.explanation: Age, integrity failures, poor cleaning recovery, and quality shortfalls all concentrate in Banks 1 and 2, and the pilot replacement confirms new modules restore performance there. Banks 3 and 4 perform near baseline, which contradicts replacing them first or replacing everything at once.

nextClue.prompt: Which record best supports the staged replacement decision?

options.label: Archived bank by bank integrity, permeability, and cleaning recovery summary
Archived membrane purchase price list
Archived plant total flow log

nextClue.explanation: The correct record directly tests the supported explanation against the alternatives.

clueText.nc-a: The summary shows failure indicators only in Banks 1 and 2 and healthy performance in Banks 3 and 4.
clueText.nc-b: Prices show cost only and do not show which banks have failed.
clueText.nc-c: Total flow hides bank level differences that drive the decision.

tasks.prompt: After a membrane supplier change, Train 2 cleaning frequency doubled while Train 1 on the original membranes stayed on its normal schedule.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Class 4 water treatment utility record. Steady operation unless noted. Archived plant, laboratory, and management records are available for review.

evidence.label: Both trains share feed water, flux, and cleaning chemicals and procedures.
Train 2 normalized permeability falls twice as fast as Train 1 between cleans in a paired 8 week comparison.
A side by side bench test of fibres from both trains in the same foulant solution shows Train 2 fibres foul 45 percent faster.
Feed quality, temperature, and backwash settings were matched across the comparison period.
Swapping the cleaning chemical batch between trains did not change which train fouled faster.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The replacement membrane material on Train 2 fouls faster under identical conditions
The cleaning chemical batch is defective for Train 2 only
Train 2 receives dirtier feed water than Train 1
Operators clean Train 2 on a different procedure

inference.explanation: Shared feed and procedures, a paired plant comparison, and a controlled bench test all point to the membrane material itself. Swapping chemical batches did not move the problem, which rules out the chemical batch, and shared feed rules out dirtier water for one train.

nextClue.prompt: Which record best confirms the material difference?

options.label: Archived cleaning chemical delivery invoices
Archived feed turbidity log for the common header
Archived paired train fouling rate log paired with the bench fibre test report

nextClue.explanation: The correct record directly tests the supported explanation against the alternatives.

clueText.nc-a: Invoices show deliveries, not fouling behaviour.
clueText.nc-b: Common header turbidity was the same for both trains.
clueText.nc-c: Fouling rate is double on Train 2 in both the plant pairing and the bench test on the same solution.

tasks.prompt: A utility membrane plant reports rising energy use per cubic metre, and a fleet audit compares specific energy across four identical trains.

Membrane permeability on Train 2 matches the other trains after temperature correction.

All trains need higher pressure because feed quality worsened
The energy meter on Train 2 is faulty and pressure is normal
A faulty valve positioner is throttling Train 2 and wasting pumping energy, not membrane fouling

inference.explanation: Permeability matches the fleet, which argues against fouling, while the partly closed valve, high feed pressure, and the repair trial all localize the loss to throttling. A faulty energy meter would not explain the measured pressure difference or the trial result.

nextClue.prompt: Which record best confirms the throttling loss?

options.label: Archived raw water turbidity log
Archived Train 2 valve position and feed pressure trend before and after the positioner repair
Archived membrane cleaning log

nextClue.explanation: The correct record directly tests the supported explanation against the alternatives.

clueText.nc-a: Turbidity was common to all trains and cannot explain one train.
clueText.nc-b: Valve opening and pressure normalized together after the repair and specific energy fell to the fleet value.
clueText.nc-c: Cleaning dates do not line up with the pressure change.

Archived storage level log for one peak hour

nextClue.explanation: The correct record directly tests the supported explanation against the alternatives.
